reference.source: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics / Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
clinicalPearls: A phenotype (a sequence rather than a single disease) resulting from reduced foetal movement in utero, presenting with multiple congenital contractures
The hallmark tetrad is foetal akinesia, multiple joint contractures, pulmonary hypoplasia and craniofacial anomalies
Polyhydramnios reflects impaired foetal swallowing, and intrauterine growth restriction and a short umbilical cord are common
Pulmonary hypoplasia, caused by absent foetal breathing movements, is the usual cause of death and is frequently lethal in the neonatal period
Facial features include hypertelorism, a small mouth, micrognathia, low-set ears and depressed nasal tip
It is aetiologically heterogeneous, arising from any process that limits foetal movement (neurogenic, myopathic, neuromuscular junction, connective tissue or restrictive uterine causes)
Recurrence risk depends on the underlying cause, so establishing the aetiology is essential for counselling
reference.pathophysiology: Pena-Shokeir syndrome is the end result of the foetal akinesia deformation sequence: any insult that reduces or abolishes foetal movement during development produces a stereotyped set of secondary deformations. Immobility permits periarticular fibrosis and multiple joint contractures, absent breathing movements prevent normal lung expansion and cause pulmonary hypoplasia, and reduced swallowing leads to polyhydramnios and a small mouth. Causes are heterogeneous and may lie anywhere along the neuromuscular axis (central nervous system, anterior horn cell, peripheral nerve, neuromuscular junction or muscle) or in restrictive intrauterine conditions such as oligohydramnios or uterine anomaly.
additionalDifferentials: Amyoplasia (survivable form) and other arthrogryposis syndromes
additionalInvestigations: Detailed prenatal ultrasound documenting reduced foetal movement, contractures and polyhydramnios
Postnatal or postmortem examination and clinical photographs to define the phenotype
Muscle and nerve histology to identify a myopathic or neurogenic basis
Molecular genetic testing, including panels for neuromuscular and neuromuscular-junction genes
Chromosomal microarray or karyotype to exclude aneuploidy
Maternal testing for myasthenia or myotonic dystrophy where relevant
redFlags: Neonatal respiratory failure from pulmonary hypoplasia, often not survivable
Antenatal signs of severe akinesia and polyhydramnios indicating poor prognosis
Feeding failure and inability to protect the airway
Findings suggesting a treatable maternal cause such as myasthenia gravis
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is generally poor, with many affected infants stillborn or dying in the neonatal period from pulmonary hypoplasia; management is largely supportive and palliative, with counselling directed by the identified underlying cause.
pitfalls: Treating Pena-Shokeir as a single diagnosis rather than searching for its underlying cause
Failing to counsel on recurrence, which varies widely by aetiology
Overlooking a treatable maternal condition such as myasthenia gravis
Not offering postmortem examination and genetic testing to guide future pregnancies
references: Emery and Rimoin's Principles and Practice of Medical Genetics
Gorlin's Syndromes of the Head and Neck
